newsitem.title: UK: Feud mars British opposition leader election race.
newsitem.headline: Feud mars British opposition leader election race.

text.p: A feud between Britain's ex-interior minister and the woman who was his main lieutenant injected new levels of viciousness into the battle to replace John Major as Conservative Party leader on Tuesday.
But the efforts of Ann Widdecombe to discredit her former boss Michael Howard left her deserted even by some of her political friends.
Howard is a right-wing challenger in the field of six candidates for the job Major will quit after the landslide victory of the Labour Party in the May 1 general election.
But Howard's campaign has been disrupted by Widdecombe, who has threatened to make a personal statement to parliament denouncing a controversial decision he made in 1995.

Widdecombe plans to claim Howard misled parliament in a statement he made about the sacking of Derek Lewis as director-general of the prison service -- a decision which Lewis himself has said left Widdecombe in tears.

Howard denies any impropriety. He told BBC television: "My colleagues in the parliamentary party will look at these allegations and will judge them for what they are worth. There is no truth in them whatever."
A report in the Daily Mail newspaper on Tuesday claimed that Lewis had formed a close personal bond with Widdecombe, 49, who has never married, when she was a junior minister at the Home Office.

He had "wooed her with bouquets, chocolates and private dinners" in "one of the most unusual professional alliances Whitehall (the area of London which houses most ministries) had ever seen," wrote journalist Paul Eastham.
Widdecombe angrily denied Eastham's report. She said it probably stemmed from information fed him by the Howard camp, and demanded her former boss either deny it or apologise.

"Nobody woos me with chocolates because they have far too much respect for the width of my figure...and as far as dinners go, the first time I had dinner with Derek Lewis was months after his sacking," she told BBC radio.
But Widdecombe was disowned by Peter Lilley, the candidate for the leadership whom she has publicly backed.
He told journalists that if she had complaints about Howard she should have voiced them privately to Major, still caretaker leader of the party.
Lilley said Widdecombe had never been part of his campaign team -- and certainly would not join it now.

"She had expressed some sympathy for my endeavours. Had she not been determined to publicise her criticisms of a fellow candidate...I would have quite liked to have had her round this table as part of my campaign."
